**Source:** `.github/SECURITY.md`

# Security policy

Tusk's Tomes is a **local-first** application — it runs on your machine, binds only to `127.0.0.1` by default, has no telemetry, and only ever sends text (never audio) to the LLM provider you configure. The risk surface is small but not zero. This page lays out what's covered, what isn't, and what you can do to keep yourself safe.

## Trust model in one paragraph

Apart from the model providers you choose, Tomes runs on your machine. API keys are encrypted at rest at `{configDir}/providers.enc` using AES-256-GCM with a scrypt-derived key bound to your machine identity (hostname + username + platform) and a salt kept beside the file. The Express server binds to loopback by default; all `/api/*` state-changing routes are same-origin gated to block drive-by-CSRF; chronicle save paths are sanitised against traversal; the local-LLM proxy refuses any target outside loopback or RFC-1918 LAN. No audio leaves the host: Whisper runs in a separate Python process on your machine when the audio module is installed.

![A drawing of the moving parts and the wires between them. Inside your computer, the Tomes page in your browser gets your stored keys from a host-only route and talks over loopback, which never touches the network, to the Tomes server on 127.0.0.1. Beside the server sit the keystore, Whisper, the claude and codex command-line tools and a local runner. A dashed wire runs to your network, where another device and a runner on another machine sit. That wire is plain HTTP, so anyone on that network can read or change the traffic; a figure inside the network box marks someone who can listen. It is used only if you open Tomes to the LAN or point at a runner there. A solid wire with a padlock marked HTTPS runs to the internet, to Gemini and OpenRouter and to Anthropic and OpenAI: a listener on the way sees only scrambled traffic, and the provider reads what you send it.](../docs/assets/diagrams/threat-model-wires.svg)

Session text goes only to the model providers you choose. The page in your browser calls Gemini and OpenRouter itself over HTTPS, with keys it fetches from a host-only route, and Claude Code or Codex make their own HTTPS calls. The rest of the outbound traffic carries none of your session: package installs, a one-off model download, the update check and OpenRouter's public lists of models and provider data policies, which you can switch to manual updates ([the full list](../docs/security/overview.md#what-goes-over-the-network)).

> **Want the reasoning rather than the summary?** [Security architecture](https://github.com/KochiTusker/Tusks-Tomes/blob/main/.github/security-architecture.md)
> documents the trust boundaries, the layered request gates, and a decision record for each
> control — including what each one deliberately does *not* cover.

## What this is NOT

Tusk's Tomes is **not** a SaaS, **not** a multi-tenant service, and **not** a hardened public-internet-facing application. The threat model below assumes a single user, on their own machine, on a network they reasonably trust. Running Tomes on a shared workstation, on a server, or on a public IP is outside the design — possible with care, but you take responsibility for the gates Tomes doesn't provide (auth, TLS, audit logging).

It also is not a substitute for keeping your provider account secure (rotate keys regularly; set spending caps) or your machine secure (full-disk encryption, OS updates, careful what you `pip install`).

The risks we know about, which of them are deliberate trade-offs and which are gaps we intend to close, are listed in plain English at the top of [the security overview](../docs/security/overview.md#known-risks-and-limitations).

---

## STRIDE — base product, no add-ons

The base install (paste-a-transcript chronicling with a cloud LLM) is the smallest attack surface. The drawing is the short version, by who might try something; the table below names each STRIDE category, the realistic risk in this product, what the code does about it today, and what's still on you.

![A drawing of four would-be intruders around your computer, which holds Tomes and your stored API keys. Each has an arrow toward it that is either stopped at a barrier or gets through. A web page open in your browser is stopped: writes from another site are refused, and on the default address a Host-name check also turns away pages that point their domain at your computer. A device on your network is stopped by default, because by default Tomes cannot be reached from the network at all; if you open Tomes to the LAN it can read, and with LAN writes on it can change things, but it never reaches your stored keys, the provider test, updates, saving settings, or running Claude Code or Codex. A copy of your config folder stays shut: the key file does not open under another host name or user name. A program running as you gets in, drawn in orange because it gets through: it can read your keys, because the app decrypts them itself; rotate them at the provider if you suspect it.](../docs/assets/diagrams/threat-model-who.svg)

| Category | Risk | Mitigation in place | Your responsibility |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Spoofing** | A malicious page in your browser tries to use Tomes's API to drive an action (install an add-on, save settings, exfil keys via a bug). | Server binds to `127.0.0.1` by default; same-origin middleware on `/api/*` rejects cross-origin POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE; the keys endpoint returns nothing on the public summary route. The `/api/provider-keys` route (decrypted keystore) is also gated by a loopback-only middleware that checks the actual TCP peer (not the spoofable `Host` header) — visiting LAN devices get a 403 even when `TUSKS_HOST=0.0.0.0` is set. **A LAN-write gate additionally blocks all non-GET requests from LAN sources unless the user explicitly sets `TUSKS_LAN_WRITES=1`** — so opting into LAN exposure gives visitors read-only access by default. | If you opt into LAN exposure (`TUSKS_HOST=0.0.0.0`), your stored keys are still safe and LAN visitors can only BROWSE (read chronicles, transcripts, lists); they can't upload or change anything unless you also set `TUSKS_LAN_WRITES=1`. LAN traffic is plain HTTP, so only do this on trusted home / office networks; never on public Wi-Fi. See [the security overview](../docs/security/overview.md) for the plain-English version. |
| **Tampering** | Browser script modifies persisted settings (routing, glossary, profiles). | Same-origin gate on every state-changing route; keystore is AES-256-GCM and the decrypted bundle never appears in any public response. | Keep your browser sandboxed — don't paste untrusted JS into the devtools console; don't install browser extensions you haven't vetted. |
| **Repudiation** | A user denies having modified state. | N/A in a single-user local app — there's no auth boundary to repudiate within. | N/A. |
| **Information disclosure** | An attacker who has read access to your config directory + your machine identity (hostname + username + platform) can decrypt `providers.enc`. | The decryption key is machine-bound — a copied `providers.enc` does not decrypt on a machine with a different host name or user name. Atomic writes (rename-from-tmp) prevent half-written exposure during saves. | Don't share `{configDir}/providers.enc`; if your machine is compromised, **rotate your provider keys immediately** (revoke + reissue at each provider's console). The keystore is obfuscation, not high-grade crypto. |
| **Denial of service** | An LLM provider exhausts its quota mid-run; the pipeline fails halfway through. | For Gemini, the rate-limit dialog catches quota errors mid-pipeline and offers four user-controlled paths (stop and export / slow down 3× / pause and save / switch to the paid key). On-disk checkpoints let you resume tomorrow. | Watch your provider dashboard — Tomes can pause your run, but it won't alert you to billing surprises. Set spending caps at the provider for paid keys. |
| **Elevation of privilege** | An attacker tries to escalate from in-Tomes capability to OS capability. | No auth boundaries exist within the app (no users, no roles), so there is no "privilege" to escalate to within Tomes itself. The server runs as your user account, with your user account's filesystem permissions. | Run Tomes as a regular user, not root / admin. Don't `sudo bash setup.sh` — the script refuses sudo for exactly this reason. |

### Path-traversal + injection — the boring-but-important bits

- The chronicle save endpoint sanitises the campaign name (strips `\/:*?"<>|` + control characters) and resolves against `<repo>/Sessions/` before writing, so a malicious campaign string can't escape the directory.
- The docs viewer (`/api/docs/:slug`) uses an allowlist-based slug→path Map built at startup; there is no string-concatenation of user input with disk paths.
- Run-checkpoint IDs (`/api/runs/:id`) are validated against `/^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$/` — any other shape returns 400 before reaching disk.
- The `/api/sessions/:id/*` endpoints validate `:id` against the same regex.

These don't appear in the STRIDE table because they're "doors stay closed" rather than distinct categories — but they're load-bearing pieces of the same baseline.

---

## Add-on-specific implications

Installing Audio Transcription widens the surface in narrow, documented ways. It is the only module that installs anything, and can be installed, toggled off, or uninstalled at any time from **Settings → Transcription**. The remaining modules ship with the app and add no files to your disk.

### Audio Transcription

Adds a Python venv at `<repo>/vendor/python-venv/` (about 1.5–2.5 GB) and runs `faster-whisper` in a separate Python process for transcription. **No audio leaves the host.**

Additional risk: the venv has Python's normal filesystem capabilities — if the venv is tampered with, a compromised package could read anything your user account can read. Mitigation: install only via Settings → Transcription (which uses the bundled setup scripts at `scripts/whisper/setup.ps1` / `.sh`; PyTorch is installed from a version range, not one exact version); don't `pip install` random packages into `vendor/python-venv/`. The bundled `requirements.txt` is the trust boundary.

### Local LLMs

Mounts `/api/local/*` as a localhost + RFC-1918 same-origin proxy so the browser can reach Ollama / LM Studio / Unsloth (which are different ports = different origins). The proxy validates every target URL through `validateLocalBaseUrl()` (`server/platform/validators.ts`) — anything that is not loopback or a private LAN address is rejected, however the address is written. It is **not** an open proxy.

Additional risk: if you set `TUSKS_HOST=0.0.0.0` *and* `TUSKS_LAN_WRITES=1`, another device on the same LAN could route requests through your local runner. Mitigation: keep `TUSKS_HOST=127.0.0.1` (the default) unless you genuinely need LAN access; never put Tomes on a public IP without an auth layer in front.

### Chronicle Personas

Built in; its only state is the `personas.json` user-authored prompt store. No new attack surface: persona templates can interpolate chronicle text via the existing `{varName}` placeholder syntax (no code execution); the default bardic voice stays available and is never editable so a broken persona can't lock you out of the pipeline.

---

## Supported versions

Tusk's Tomes is a rolling release tracking `main`. The latest commit on `main` is the only supported version. The in-app updater (**Settings → Maintenance**) keeps you current; security fixes ship there first.

## Reporting a vulnerability

**Please do not open a public GitHub issue for security problems.**

Use this private channel:

1. **GitHub's private vulnerability reporting** — open this repository on GitHub, click the **Security** tab, then **Report a vulnerability**. GitHub keeps the report private and routes it directly to the maintainers. This is currently the only supported private channel — a community Discord with a moderator-DM route is on the [roadmap](../docs/about/roadmap.md), and this section will be updated once it launches.

Please include:

- A description of the issue and its potential impact
- Reproduction steps or a proof-of-concept
- The version / commit SHA you tested against
- Any suggested remediation (optional)

We'll acknowledge within 72 hours and aim to ship a fix within 14 days for high-severity issues. We'll credit you in the release notes unless you'd prefer to stay anonymous.

For non-sensitive coordination (i.e. not a vulnerability — design questions, hardening suggestions, threat-model discussion), the [feedback form](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdxdqOhb1SQvI3fs50gMJv_Cesh2MuxUm95QO2iZia5sFhyyQ/viewform?usp=header) is fine. **Do not put vulnerability details into the form** — Google Forms is not a private channel for security reports; use GitHub's private vulnerability reporting for anything sensitive.

## Scope

In scope:

- The Express server (`server/`) and its API routes
- The encrypted keystore (`server/features/providers/services/crypto/keyStore.ts`)
- The Whisper sidecar (`scripts/whisper/`) when the audio add-on is installed
- The in-app updater (`scripts/update/`, `server/features/maintenance/routes/updater.ts`)
- The React SPA (`src/`)
- The local LLM proxy (`server/features/providers/routes/localProxy.ts`)
- The run-checkpoint storage (`server/features/pipeline/routes/runs.ts`)

Out of scope:

- Vulnerabilities in upstream dependencies (please report those to the upstream project; we'll bump as soon as a patched version ships)
- Vulnerabilities that require a malicious LLM provider you've already configured (you trust your own API key — that's a different threat model from "Tomes leaks the key")
- Social-engineering vectors that require the user to manually run arbitrary attacker-supplied code from their dashboard
- LLM prompt-injection attacks delivered through the transcript content itself — the model is the trust boundary there, not Tomes; the chronicle output is unconditionally untrusted text and should be reviewed before sharing

## Disclosure

Once a fix has shipped to `main`, we'll publish a brief security advisory on the repo. Once the community Discord launches (see [ROADMAP.md](../docs/about/roadmap.md)), security-fix announcements will also be posted in `#announcements`.

---

**Page:** https://kochitusker.github.io/Tusks-Tomes/docs/security/overview/  
**Source:** `docs/security/overview.md`

# Security and privacy

A plain-English primer for users, not developers. It tells you what's safe by default, what you can change that *could* make things less safe, and what residual risks cannot be fixed in code.

Tusk's Tomes was built on the conviction that your campaign — and your players' voices — belong on your hardware. Everything below follows from that.

## The short version

- **Session audio never leaves your computer.** Only the text transcript, the prompt and the lore text each phase uses go to the model you chose.
- **Your API keys are encrypted at rest and bound to this machine.** A copied file does not decrypt under another host name or user account.
- **The server listens only on your own computer** unless you explicitly opt into LAN access.
- **No telemetry, no analytics, no phone-home.** Ever.
- **A fresh clone holds zero credentials and zero recordings** — only source and templates.

## Known risks and limitations

These are the risks we know about, set out before you install so you can judge them for yourself. Most are deliberate trade-offs of a local-first app built for one person on their own machine; each says why, and what you can do about it. When an update closes a gap, it comes off this list. The detail behind every item is further down this page.

### On a default install

- **You trust everything you install.** Setup installs about 686 npm packages (345 of them are what a built copy needs at run time), and four of them have install scripts on Windows and Linux, five on macOS; `package.json` approves only ffmpeg-static's, which downloads an ffmpeg program from GitHub. The optional Audio Transcription module adds PyTorch, installed from a version range rather than one exact version, more Python packages from PyPI, and about 3 GB of Whisper model weights from Hugging Face the first time you transcribe. Updates arrive only when you click to check for them and apply them.
  *What you can do:* install from a release you have looked at, and read what an update brings before you apply it. *Status:* a deliberate trade-off; this is how most open-source software installs.
- **The app has no login.** It listens only on `127.0.0.1`, so other devices cannot reach it, but every program and every user account on this computer can, including the route that hands your stored keys to the page.
  *What you can do:* run Tomes under your own account on a computer you do not share, and keep that computer free of malware. *Status:* a deliberate trade-off for a single-user app on your own machine.
- **Your sessions are stored as ordinary files.** Audio, transcripts, chronicles, your glossary and your speaker names, which can include players' real names, sit unencrypted in your user profile and in the `Sessions/` folder inside the program folder.
  *What you can do:* turn on full-disk encryption, and delete sessions you no longer need. *Status:* a deliberate trade-off; your operating system's disk encryption is the protection here.
- **Your API keys have no passphrase.** They are encrypted with a key built from this computer's host name, user name and platform and a salt kept beside them. A copied file does not open on another computer, but anything running as you can read them.
  *What you can do:* set a spending cap at each provider, and rotate your keys if anything looks wrong. *Status:* a deliberate trade-off, so the app can start without asking you for a password.
- **Two requests leave without you pressing Run.** Tomes checks two public lists from OpenRouter at most once a day: its models, so new models and current prices reach the cost estimates and the model picker, and each provider's data policy. The requests carry nothing of yours.
  *What you can do:* untick **Keep the model list up to date automatically** in the Model lists strip under **Settings → Providers & models**. Tomes then keeps using the list it has and only contacts openrouter.ai when you press Re-check. *Status:* on by default; your choice.
- **What you send, the provider reads.** When you press Run, the transcript, the prompts and the lore each phase needs go over HTTPS to the providers you chose, under their own privacy terms. Audio never leaves your computer.
  *What you can do:* route Ground, Audit and Extras to a local model, so that text stays here; the chronicle and the condensed recap always go to a cloud model or a subscription. *Status:* how the app works.
- **Codex can read files on your computer.** When a phase runs through Codex, it works in its read-only sandbox, which stops it writing files but not reading them, so a transcript with planted instructions could try to make it read something. (Claude Code runs these calls with its tools, its MCP servers and your personal settings switched off.)
  *What you can do:* read a chronicle before you share it. *Status:* a deliberate trade-off.
- **Players can plant instructions in what they say.** With Gemini, OpenRouter or Claude Code, that can only change the text that comes back; the app shows model output as plain text, so it cannot run anything in the page.
  *What you can do:* read a chronicle before you post it. *Status:* inherent in sending a transcript to a language model.

### If you turn on LAN access

LAN access is off by default. These apply only once you set `TUSKS_HOST`.

- **Traffic on your network is plain HTTP.** Anyone on the network can read it, and a device that gets in the middle can change it. With `TUSKS_HOST=0.0.0.0`, any device on the network can read your sessions; with `TUSKS_LAN_WRITES=1` as well, it can change them, start the Audio Transcription install and send prompts through your local runner. Your stored keys and the host-only routes stay on the host either way.
  *What you can do:* use LAN access only on a network you trust, and turn it off when you leave; for anything wider, put an authenticating, encrypted proxy in front. *Status:* a deliberate trade-off.
- **Web pages you visit can reach Tomes through your network address.** On the default address a Host-name check turns such pages away; with LAN access on, that check is not active.
  *What you can do:* turn LAN access off when you are not using it. *Status:* a deliberate trade-off; LAN access is off by default.
- **Keys placed in `.env` are built into the page.** `VITE_` and `PAID_` values from `.env` become part of the page your browser loads, and with LAN access on, other devices load the same page.
  *What you can do:* save your keys in **Settings → Providers & models** rather than in `.env`. *Status:* a deliberate trade-off; Settings is the normal place for keys.

More detail: [what goes over the network](#what-goes-over-the-network), [what the keystore protects you from](#what-the-encrypted-keystore-protects-you-from), [LAN access step by step](#cross-device-lan-access-tusks_host--tusks_lan_writes--i-want-to-use-tomes-from-my-tablet--phone--laptop-on-the-same-wi-fi) and [residual risks](#residual-risks-we-cannot-fix-in-code).

## Out of the box, you're fine if…

- You installed by running `setup.bat` (Windows) or `bash setup.sh` (macOS/Linux).
- You open the app at <http://localhost:5173> on the same machine you installed it on.
- You added your API keys via **Settings → Providers & models**.

There's nothing else to configure. The app talks to the LLM provider(s) you configured and to any local LLM runner you run (Ollama / LM Studio / Unsloth). The only other traffic is the short list under [What goes over the network](#what-goes-over-the-network): package installs, one-off model downloads, the update check and a public list of models.

## What's automatically protected

- **Your API keys are encrypted and locked to this machine.** The decryption key is derived from your hostname + username + platform, so a copy of the keystore file does not decrypt on a computer with a different host name or user name.
- **The web interface only listens on your own computer by default.** Other devices on your Wi-Fi cannot see it.
- **Even if you opt into LAN exposure, your keys stay private.** The route that returns the decrypted keys is loopback-only — visiting devices on the LAN can see the UI but get a 403 (refused) on the keys route. Inference still runs on your host machine.
- **Documents loaded into the Help tab are HTML-sanitised.** A future hostile update couldn't slip a `<script>` tag in and steal your keys via the UI.

## Things you might change that have trade-offs

### Cross-device LAN access (`TUSKS_HOST` + `TUSKS_LAN_WRITES`) — "I want to use Tomes from my tablet / phone / laptop on the same Wi-Fi"

Tusk's Tomes binds to `127.0.0.1` by default — only the machine running it can reach the UI. Two environment variables let you opt into broader access on your own network. They're independent toggles; the second only matters if the first is set.

#### Step 1 — should you turn this on at all?

**Turn it ON if any of these apply:**
- Your Tomes machine is in another room (basement PC, study desktop) and you want to read chronicles from your phone / tablet on the couch.
- You have a home server and want every device in the house to reach it.
- A different machine on your network has the audio recording you want to upload (e.g. you record on a laptop, run Tomes on a desktop).
- You want a player to view session transcripts in real time from their own device while you GM.

**Keep it OFF (the default) if any of these apply:**
- You only use Tomes on the same machine it's installed on.
- You're on a network you don't fully control: shared apartment Wi-Fi, dorm network, hotel / café / airport / library / conference Wi-Fi.
- You have IoT devices, smart TVs, or guest devices on your network that you wouldn't want browsing your chronicle.
- You're not sure. The default is safe; you can always flip it on later.

#### Step 2 — how to set it on (Windows, PowerShell)

```powershell
# Permanent for this user account (persists across reboots):
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("TUSKS_HOST", "0.0.0.0", "User")

# OR — just for the current PowerShell session (resets when you close the window):
$env:TUSKS_HOST = "0.0.0.0"

# Then restart the Tomes server. Open from your other device at:
#   http://<your-host-machine-IP>:5173
# To find your host machine's IP: open PowerShell on it and run `ipconfig`.
```

On macOS / Linux: `export TUSKS_HOST=0.0.0.0` then restart the server. To make it permanent, add the line to `~/.bashrc` / `~/.zshrc`.

When Tomes restarts with this set, the boot banner spells out exactly what's enabled (read-only or read+write) so you can confirm.

#### Step 3 — `TUSKS_HOST=0.0.0.0` alone (read-only LAN access — recommended starting point)

![A drawing in two parts. At the top, a dashed box for this computer, the host, says that by default only this computer opens Tomes. It lists what always stays on the host whatever you set: API keys and the Test button, the in-app updater, saving app settings, and starting a local runner. Below it, a dashed box for devices on your Wi-Fi holds two boxes side by side, and a dashed arrow runs from each up to the host, labelled that devices get a 403 for that list. The first box, with a laptop and an eye, is TUSKS_HOST=0.0.0.0: a device can read chronicles, transcripts, live progress and .sbv downloads. The second, in orange, with a laptop and a pencil, is TUSKS_LAN_WRITES=1 as well: a device can also write, meaning upload audio, save, edit, delete, install Audio Transcription and download .docx files.](../assets/diagrams/who-on-your-network.svg)

A device can also browse the session list, the system info, the add-ons list and the Help / Docs tab. Writes, including the `.docx` download, answer 403 in this mode, and the host-only list never opens to the network.

This is the "view from the couch" mode. It's the right setting for the vast majority of cross-device use cases.

#### Step 4 — `TUSKS_HOST=0.0.0.0` + `TUSKS_LAN_WRITES=1` (read+write LAN access — only if you actually need it)

Add this second variable only if you genuinely need to **upload, save, or modify content** from another device:

```powershell
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("TUSKS_LAN_WRITES", "1", "User")
# Restart Tomes. The boot banner reads "LAN writes (uploads, settings edits, saves): ENABLED".
```

With both flags on:

The second lane in the drawing adds the writes. Two details it does not carry: running the pipeline from another device works with a local runner only (phases routed to a cloud model need the stored keys, which only the host can fetch, and the Claude Code and Codex routes answer the host only), and installing or removing Audio Transcription runs the install on your host.

The host-only list is the architectural backstop: even with full LAN-write access, anything that reads your stored credentials, uses them, starts a local runner on your host, or runs the updater stays loopback-only, as do Unsloth credentials, the dev-mode toggle and saving app settings. The boot banner explicitly tells you this.

#### Step 5 — security implications, in plain language

Setting **`TUSKS_HOST=0.0.0.0` alone** means: anyone connected to your Wi-Fi who knows your machine's IP can BROWSE everything Tomes shows you. They can read your campaign chronicles, see the players' real names if you've captured them, and watch live transcription as it happens. They cannot break anything or take anything — but **they can read the prose**.

Setting **both flags** means: anyone connected to your Wi-Fi who knows your machine's IP can also CHANGE everything. They can upload garbage audio, delete chronicles, edit your glossary so the next chronicle calls everyone by the wrong name, or push their own prompts through your local runner.

**In both modes**, your stored API keys stay on the host — they're encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a machine-bound key AND the route that hands them out is loopback-only AND the route that triggers an outbound provider test is loopback-only. A device on your network cannot read them, even with write access to everything else.

**The threat model that makes LAN exposure safe:** you trust every device that's allowed on your Wi-Fi. That includes the smart TV, the smart speakers, the kid's tablet, the visiting friend's laptop, and any IoT thing you've connected. If you're not confident about all of those, leave the toggle off.

#### Step 6 — turning it off

When you're done (e.g. you took the laptop to a coffee shop):

```powershell
# Wipe the persistent setting:
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("TUSKS_HOST", $null, "User")
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("TUSKS_LAN_WRITES", $null, "User")

# Restart Tomes. The boot banner should NOT mention LAN exposure.
```

The toggle is binary; there's no "trust this device only" partial mode. If you need that level of granularity, put an authenticating reverse proxy (Caddy with basic auth, Tailscale with ACLs) in front of Tomes — but that's beyond the scope of the default install.

### Running on a server / cloud VM

Tusk's Tomes was not designed for this. There is no login system, no audit log, no user accounts. If you put it on a public IP, **anyone on the internet** who finds the address can use the app, browse transcripts, and burn through your LLM credits. We do not have a deployment guide for this configuration. If you go ahead anyway, put an authenticating reverse proxy (Caddy with basic auth, Cloudflare Tunnel with access policies, etc.) in front of it.

### Local-LLM with a non-default backend URL

If you point Unsloth/LM Studio/Ollama at a custom URL via Settings, that URL is validated to be a local / private LAN address. We refuse to send credentials to a public IP. There is a small TOCTOU window where DNS-rebinding can theoretically slip past — see "Residual risks" below.

## What goes over the network

![A drawing of what leaves your machine. At the top, a dashed box for your machine lists what is never sent anywhere: your recordings and Whisper, the files Tomes saves, and local runners, which stay on this computer or your LAN. Below it, one arrow runs to each destination. The model you chose receives the transcript, prompt and lore when you press Run, and just the key when you press Test; Claude Code and Codex go through their own CLI. Package sites (npm, GitHub, PyPI, PyTorch and Hugging Face) are contacted once, at install or first use. github.com is contacted when you press Check for updates, for a git fetch. openrouter.ai is asked for its public model list and its provider data policies at most once a day, with nothing of yours sent; you can switch automatic updates off in Settings.](../assets/diagrams/what-goes-over-the-network.svg)

Two more cases are not in the drawing. Opening the Local LLMs panel or pressing **Detect again** sends a capability probe to a loopback or private-LAN address only (validated). `npm run smoke-test` sends a small health-check prompt to every provider you have configured.

**That is the entire outbound list.** No background pings, no usage stats, no
"anonymous" metrics.

> [!TIP]
> **Local runners and Whisper send nothing out while they work.** Audio decoding,
> transcription and segment timing all happen on your own CPU or GPU. Whisper's
> only network use is the one-off package and model downloads in the table above,
> and the local-model proxy validates that every target URL is loopback or private LAN
> before it will forward anything. It is not an open proxy.

## What the encrypted keystore protects you from

![A drawing of how the key to your stored API keys is made, and who can open the file. At the top, four boxes (host name, user name, platform and a random salt) feed one box, locked to this computer and this user. That produces providers.enc in your config folder. Below, under the question who can open that file, a purple padlock box labelled stays shut covers a providers.enc copied to another computer or account, such as a backup, cloud sync or a stray copy. An orange terminal box labelled opens covers a program running as you on this computer, because the app decrypts the keys for itself.](../assets/diagrams/what-the-keystore-protects.svg)

Because the key comes from the host name, user name and platform, a `providers.enc` copied by a backup, cloud sync or anything else does not open where those differ. The file lives in the config directory, not the repo.

> [!CAUTION]
> It does **not** protect you from someone with a live shell on your machine as
> your user. At that point they can simply ask the running app for the keys.
> That is the standard threat-model boundary for any local-first app that stores
> credentials, and no amount of encryption at rest moves it.

## Tusk's Vault interop is purely filesystem-based

Sending a finished chronicle to Tusk's Vault copies the markdown into
`<vault>/Lore/Tomes/<campaign>/<file>.md`. That is a copy operation — no
network, no API, no third party. The two projects find each other by sibling
directory detection; see [the Vault guide](../extras/tusks-vault.md).

## Residual risks we cannot fix in code

- **The keystore is a lock against copied files, not a password.** The cipher is AES-256-GCM, but the key comes from your host name, user name and platform plus a salt kept beside the file, so the app opens it without asking you. If your computer is compromised (malware running as you, or another user with admin access), the attacker can read the decrypted keys at runtime — the app decrypts them itself and hands them to the browser to make LLM calls. Rotate your API keys at the provider's dashboard immediately if you suspect compromise. This is true of every local-first app that stores credentials.
- **DNS rebinding has a small (≤60 s) window** for the local-LLM proxy. We resolve the hostname once and cache it; the actual `fetch()` re-resolves. A hostile DNS server answering 127.0.0.1 to our lookup, then a public IP to the fetch, could in theory slip through. Mitigated by pointing local-LLM at a literal IP (`192.168.1.42`) or `localhost` rather than a hostname.
- **Prompt injection** through the transcript content is on the LLM, not on us. A player who knows the app is being used could put adversarial text in the chat that tricks the model into producing weird chronicle content. Read chronicles before sharing them publicly.
- **You ARE the security boundary** between Tomes and the public internet. No login, no audit log, no per-IP rate-limits. Keep your machine secure (OS updates, antivirus on Windows, full-disk encryption); Tomes inherits your machine's security posture.

## What you need to do

Three things, total:

1. **Add API keys** at **Settings → Providers & models**. The app won't generate chronicles without one.
2. **Keep your machine secure** — OS updates, antivirus on Windows, full-disk encryption. Tomes inherits your machine's security.
3. **Rotate your API keys at the provider's dashboard** every few months, or immediately if anything weird happens (charges you don't recognise, a colleague using your laptop without permission, suspected malware).

## Next

- [What it installs, and what could go wrong](what-it-installs.md) — the honest version
- [Security policy](../../.github/SECURITY.md) — threat model in STRIDE form, and how to report a vulnerability
- [Configuration](../settings/configuration.md) — exactly where every file lives

---

**Page:** https://kochitusker.github.io/Tusks-Tomes/docs/security/what-it-installs/  
**Source:** `docs/security/what-it-installs.md`

# What it installs

Short version: I'm a GM who got fed up and wrote this for my own table. This
page is me telling you exactly what it does to your computer, including the
parts I'm not thrilled about, because you're about to run a stranger's code and
you deserve to make that call with the facts.

I'd rather be transparent than reassuring. Where something could bite you, it's
below.

## Where this came from

I wanted a record of my sessions. Not minutes — the actual story. The bit where
the rogue did something monumentally stupid and it somehow worked. The joke
that had everyone crying. The line the DM delivered that made the table go
quiet.

The existing options didn't fit. Meeting transcribers are built for standups:
you get a transcript and a bulleted summary, for $15 a month, forever, in
somebody else's cloud. And none of them have the faintest idea who Eamon is —
they'd hear the name, invent a spelling, and confidently use the wrong one for
three hours straight.

So this got built. It's a niche tool for a niche group of people: GMs who want
their campaign written up properly, grounded in their own names and lore, on
their own machine, without a subscription. If that's you, welcome. If you need
something polished and enterprise-grade, I'd genuinely point you elsewhere —
this is one person's project, and the rest of this page is about what that
means for you.

## It's a work in progress, and it's tested on one PC

It's not a commercial product with a QA department. It's
tested on my machine, which runs Windows and has an NVIDIA card, and that shows
up in what I can honestly claim:

| Area | How well tested |
|---|---|
| Windows | My daily driver. Well exercised. |
| Linux / macOS | **Not tested.** It should work — I haven't proven it. |
| Cloud providers (Gemini, OpenRouter) | Well exercised — this is the path I use every session. |
| Audio transcription (Whisper) | Exercised on an NVIDIA GPU. CPU-only works, but slowly. |
| Claude Code add-on | Exercised. |
| Codex add-on | Partially tested. |
| Local LLMs add-on | **Partially tested** — I don't have the VRAM to run anything above 4B. |
| Obsidian vault add-on | Exercised, including the writes described below. |

I don't expect anything serious to go wrong, but "I don't expect" isn't a
guarantee and I'm not going to dress it up as one. What I have tried hard to
do is make sure that if something *does* go wrong, it wrecks files this app
created — not the files you already had. Most of this page is about how well
that holds up, and where it doesn't.

---

## What you need before you start (I can't install these for you)

Being straight about this, because it's the bit that catches people out: there
is no one-click installer yet. You need a couple of things already on your
machine, and **Tusk's Tomes deliberately does not install them for you** — a
setup script that silently installs system-wide software is exactly the kind of
thing I wouldn't want running on my own PC. It checks, tells you the exact
command, and stops.

| You need | When | If it's missing |
|---|---|---|
| **Node.js 22+** (Node 20+ for releases before 2.7.0) | Always. Nothing runs without it. | Setup stops and prints `winget install OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS`. |
| **Git** | To download the project in the first place; setup checks for it too. | Setup stops and prints the install command. |
| **Python 3.10, 3.11 or 3.12** | **Only** for the audio-transcription add-on. | The core app is completely fine without it. |

Two things worth knowing:

- **Python 3.10 to 3.12 are the versions I have verified** for transcription.
  3.13 is untested: the PyTorch builds it needs arrived late, and nobody has
  run the whole stack on it here. Setup checks your version and warns rather
  than blocking, while the in-app Install check stops on anything outside
  3.10–3.12. If a transcription install fails on 3.13, make 3.12 the first
  `python` on your PATH and run it again.
- **You do not need Visual Studio Build Tools**, whatever older guides say.
  Nothing in the dependency tree compiles native code.

So yes — realistically this is still a "you're comfortable installing Node and
running a `.bat` file" project. I'd like that not to be true, and a proper
standalone installer that handles the whole thing is on the
[roadmap](../about/roadmap.md). Right now it isn't done, and pretending otherwise
would just waste your evening.

## What it installs, and where

There's no installer. You clone a folder and run `setup.bat` (or `setup.sh`).
No MSI, no elevation prompt, nothing added to Windows itself.

| Location | What | Size |
|---|---|---|
| `<the folder you cloned into>` | The program itself. | ~8 MB |
| `…\node_modules` | JavaScript libraries, fetched by `npm install`. | several hundred MB (about 450 MB on a Windows test machine) |
| `…\dist`, `…\dist-server` | Built output, only if you run a build. | ~5 MB |
| `…\vendor\python-venv` | Python, PyTorch and the speech-to-text libraries. **Only if you install the audio add-on.** The model weights are fetched on first use into the Hugging Face cache, not here. | about 1.5–2.5 GB |
| `…\Sessions\<campaign>\` | Your finished chronicles, as Markdown. | small |
| `%APPDATA%\tusks-tomes` | Settings, glossary, speaker names, encrypted API key, paused-run checkpoints. | small |
| `%LOCALAPPDATA%\tusks-tomes` | Session recordings, transcripts, the saved-chronicle library, cached probe results. | large, if you upload audio |

![Three places Tusk's Tomes keeps files. The program folder holds the program code and is replaced by an update, but your Sessions folder and .env file inside it are left alone. Your profile, outside the program folder, holds settings, keys, recordings and saved chronicles, and survives an update. Next to the program folder, Tusks-Lore holds lore notes and .docx exports, and also survives an update.](../assets/diagrams/where-files-live.svg)

Delete the cloned folder and the first five go with it; the last two stay.

### Three things I think you should understand

**`node_modules` is other people's code.** It's the standard JavaScript
dependency set from npm, and it's by far the largest body of code on your
machine that I didn't write. I can't personally vouch for all of it — nobody in
this ecosystem can. What I can tell you is that it's all listed in
`package.json`, `npm audit` will report known problems in it any time you ask,
and CI fails the build if a shipping dependency has a high-severity advisory.

**The Whisper add-on is the heavy one.** It installs Python packages including
PyTorch, plus a CUDA build if you have an NVIDIA card. It's big, it's fiddly,
and it's the step most likely to fall over on your machine. It's also entirely
optional and, apart from the model weights it fetches on first use, lives in exactly one folder.

**Your API key is encrypted, but it's still on your disk.** It's tied to this
machine — hostname, username, platform — so a copy of the file won't decrypt on a
computer with a different host name or user name. That covers a stray copy, such as a backup or a cloud-synced folder. It
doesn't defend against someone already sitting at your computer.

---

## Everything it writes outside its own folder

I'd rather list these than tell you "it all stays in one place", because that
isn't true. Every one of them happens because you asked for it.

| What it writes | Where | When |
|---|---|---|
| Settings, keys, glossary, paused-run checkpoints | `%APPDATA%\tusks-tomes` | When you change a setting or pause a run. |
| Recordings, transcripts, saved chronicles | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\tusks-tomes` | When you upload audio or finish a run. |
| Cached probe results | the platform cache folder | Throwaway; safe to delete any time. |
| Whisper model weights (about 3 GB) | `%USERPROFILE%\.cache\huggingface\hub`, or wherever `HF_HOME` points | The first time you transcribe audio. The uninstaller leaves them. |
| A `Tusks-Lore` folder **beside** the program folder | your chosen location | Only if you click "Create Tusk's Lore". |
| Files into a paired **Tusk's Vault** install | wherever you put Vault | Only if you pair them and send a chronicle across. |
| **Into your Obsidian vault** | the folder you picked | Only via three specific, opt-in buttons — see below. |

### The Obsidian vault is the one that would worry me

That folder is *your notes*. It's the only place this app writes to something
you made, and I don't take that lightly. Reading is the normal mode. There are
exactly three writes, each one started by you:

![A drawing of what Tusk's Tomes does with an Obsidian vault. At the top right is Tusk's Tomes; at the top left is a disk labelled index cache, outside the vault, and an arrow from Tomes says it keeps its index there. A second arrow from Tomes, labelled reads, points into a dashed box for your Obsidian vault. Inside the box, under Read, always, are two boxes: names and aliases, which become the entity index for Phase 1, and note bodies, which become lore for the chronicle. Under Written, only when you ask, are three gold boxes: Word and PDF notes get a .md copy beside each, Build graphify map writes a graphify-out folder, and Generate CLAUDE.md writes a file at the vault root.](../assets/diagrams/what-tomes-does-in-your-vault.svg)

The `.md` conversion is a step in Recommended Setup that copies each Word or PDF file you tick, beside the original. It never modifies or deletes your original and refuses to overwrite an existing `.md`. If a `CLAUDE.md` already exists, the generator stops and asks before replacing it.

The code that reads your vault during a normal chronicle run cannot write at
all. That's not me promising to be careful — there's a test that fails the
build if a write call ever appears in those files.

**If your vault matters to you and isn't already backed up or in git, back it
up before you first use those features.** I'd tell you that about any tool that
touches your notes, including mine.

---

## What it never does

- No registry entries, no services, no scheduled tasks, no startup items, no
  PATH changes.
- No Administrator elevation, ever. If something asks you for admin rights
  while you're installing this, it didn't come from me.
- No telemetry, no analytics, no crash reporting, no update pings. There's
  nothing to opt out of because there's nothing there. I don't know how many
  people use this and I'm fine with that.
- No account, no login, no server of mine anywhere.
- It listens on `127.0.0.1` — your machine only, not your network.

The only part of your session that leaves your computer is transcript text, with the lore text each phase uses, going to whichever AI provider you set up so it can write the chronicle. The rest of the network traffic carries none of your session content: package installs, the Whisper model download, OpenRouter's public lists of models and provider data policies (at most once a day, and you can switch that off), and the update check when you press the button. [What goes over the network](overview.md#what-goes-over-the-network) lists each one. Local models can take the grounding, audit and extras phases, and the text for those stays on your machine; the chronicle and condensed recap always go to a cloud model or a subscription CLI.

---

## What could go wrong — the things I already know about

### The folder isn't writable

The most common failure by a mile. It happens when the folder is in
`C:\Program Files`, at the root of `C:\`, on a disconnected network drive, or
being held by OneDrive or antivirus. Setup checks for this before touching
anything, so you get told rather than left with a half-finished install.

**Fix:** move the folder to Documents or Desktop and run setup again.

**Please don't "fix" it by running as Administrator.** It's the first thing
everyone tries and it makes things worse — you end up with files your normal
account can't modify, and the app fails later in far more confusing ways. This
never needs elevation.

### The Python / Whisper install falls over part-way

Python packaging is fragile and this step downloads a lot. I've seen it fail
from: no Python, Python not on PATH, no disk space, a dropped connection
mid-download, and antivirus interrupting file creation.

**How bad is it:** contained to `vendor\python-venv`. Delete that folder and
re-run the add-on install. Your system Python is never touched — the whole
reason it builds a separate environment is so a bad day here can't reach it.

### Antivirus gets involved

To a heuristic scanner, installing software looks a lot like malware: a process
creating hundreds of files fast and pulling down executables. If setup dies
with no explanation, check your antivirus history before assuming the app is
broken. All the source is public if you want to look first.

### The uninstaller genuinely deletes things

It's the one part with real destructive power, so here's how it's fenced in. It
refuses to run unless it's sitting in a real Tusk's Tomes folder. It resolves
every path through the filesystem before deleting, so a symlink can't redirect
it somewhere else. It refuses any path that isn't either inside the program
folder or under a folder named `tusks-tomes`. It makes you type
`I UNDERSTAND` before it starts. It keeps everything you authored unless you
explicitly tell it not to, and it never touches a lore folder or a custom
session folder.

It's still code, and code has bugs. **`npm run uninstall -- --dry-run` shows
you exactly what it would delete and deletes nothing.** Worth doing first.

One sharp edge I know about: it decides which folder to clean from **its own
location on disk**, not from where you run it. If you copy `uninstall.mjs`
somewhere else and run it there, it will still go after the folder it was
copied from. Run it in place with `npm run uninstall`. I know this because I
caught it out exactly that way during development.

### Platforms I can't test

On Linux or macOS you may well be the first person down that path. I don't
expect breakage, but I haven't earned the right to say more than that. If you
hit something, please tell me — that's genuinely the fastest way it gets fixed.

### Putting it on your network

By default only your own machine can reach it. Setting `TUSKS_HOST=0.0.0.0`
makes it reachable across your local network. Even then, write operations stay
off unless you separately enable them — but anyone on that network could still
read your transcripts. Only do it on a network you control.

### It runs other programs

Tusk's Tomes launches other software on your machine: Python for transcription,
`ffmpeg` (the copy bundled with the app) for audio, `nvidia-smi` to ask about your graphics card, and — if you
turn those add-ons on — the `claude`, `codex` or `ollama` commands. All with
your normal user permissions, never elevated, and all programs that are already on your machine or come with the app.

---

## Keeping the blast radius small

Things that genuinely limit what a bug of mine could reach:

- **Clone into a normal folder.** Documents or Desktop. Not Program Files, not
  a synced OneDrive folder.
- **Back up your Obsidian vault** before first using the conversion or
  generator buttons, if it isn't in version control already.
- **Run the uninstaller with `--dry-run` first.**
- **Skip add-ons you don't need.** Everything past "paste a transcript" is
  opt-in. Not installing Whisper skips a download of about 1.5–2.5 GB and the most fragile step there is.
- **Keep your lore folder outside the program folder** — that's the default, and
  it means deleting the app can never reach your notes.

---

## Don't take my word for it

It's all public at
[github.com/KochiTusker/Tusks-Tomes](https://github.com/KochiTusker/Tusks-Tomes).
If you only read four files, read these — they're the ones that actually answer
this question:

- `setup.bat` / `scripts/setup/check-deps.mjs` — everything the install does.
- `scripts/uninstall.mjs` — everything the uninstall does, guards included.
- `scripts/whisper/setup.ps1` — the Python environment build.
- `server/features/lore/services/obsidian/` — the vault code, and the read-only test that enforces
  what I claimed above.

If any of it doesn't match what you see happening, that's a bug and I want to
know: [open an issue](https://github.com/KochiTusker/Tusks-Tomes/issues/new/choose).

## Getting rid of it

```
npm run uninstall
```

It keeps everything you authored unless you pass `--purge-user-data`, and
leaves a `TUSKS-TOMES-uninstall-notes.md` in the folder listing what was
removed, what was kept and where, and which leftovers are **shared with other
software** and shouldn't be deleted just to tidy up. Move that file somewhere
safe before you delete the folder.

`npm run uninstall -- --list-locations` prints the same paths and deletes
nothing at all.

Then delete the folder. What stays outside it is what you chose to keep, plus the items in the table of things it writes outside its own folder: the Whisper model weights, a `Tusks-Lore` folder, files in a paired Vault, and anything it wrote into your Obsidian vault.

---

**Page:** https://kochitusker.github.io/Tusks-Tomes/docs/settings/configuration/  
**Source:** `docs/settings/configuration.md`

# Configuration

Two sources of config, in priority order:

1. **In-app Settings tab.** Encrypted keystore, per-phase model routing, pipeline tuning, narrator voice, and local runner endpoints. The source of truth after first save.
2. **`.env` in the repo root.** Read by the browser build only: `VITE_` and `PAID_` values (Gemini keys and model overrides) reach the app this way. Other variables (`PORT`, `TUSKS_*`, `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`) are read from the real process environment, so set those in your shell or system environment. If no keystore exists on first boot, it is seeded from `PAID_GEMINI_API_KEY`, `VITE_GEMINI_API_KEY` and `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` found in that environment; after that the encrypted store is the source of truth.

<details class="docs-section">
<summary><h2>Where things live on disk</h2></summary>
<div class="docs-section-body">


![Three places Tusk's Tomes keeps files. The program folder holds the program code and is replaced by an update, but your Sessions folder and .env file inside it are left alone. Your profile, outside the program folder, holds settings, keys, recordings and saved chronicles, and survives an update. Next to the program folder, Tusks-Lore holds lore notes and .docx exports, and also survives an update.](../assets/diagrams/where-files-live.svg)

Paths under `<repo>` are inside the program folder; `<repo>/Sessions/`, `<repo>/vendor/` and `<repo>/.env` are gitignored. `{configDir}`, `{dataDir}`, `{cacheDir}` and the Hugging Face cache are per-user and outside the repo. `<parent>/Tusks-Lore/` sits beside the repo and is shared with Tusk's Vault. Everything under `{cacheDir}` is safe to delete.

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `<repo>/Sessions/<campaign>/*.md` | Auto-saved chronicles in Markdown |
| `{dataDir}/sessions/<id>/` | Per-session audio + manifest + SBV (only used by the Audio Transcription add-on) |
| `{dataDir}/chronicle-library/<id>.json` | Saved chronicles: each finished run's chronicle, extras and condensed version |
| `{configDir}/runs/<runId>.json` | Paused-run checkpoints |
| `{configDir}/.salt` | The per-machine value the keystore key is derived from |
| `{configDir}/providers.enc` | Encrypted API keys (AES-256-GCM, machine-bound scrypt key) |
| `{configDir}/{glossary,speakers,profiles,routing}.json` | UI-edited config — glossary terms, speaker mappings, per-provider model overrides, per-phase routing |
| `{configDir}/settings.json` | App settings not covered by the files above |
| `{configDir}/personas.json` | Personas you have authored or generated. Seeded with the six presets on first read, and never deleted by the app |
| `{configDir}/model-availability.json` | Which models each configured key was measured to actually reach |
| `{configDir}/openrouter-models.json` | Cached OpenRouter model list (see Model list updates) |
| `{configDir}/openrouter-providers.json` | Cached OpenRouter provider data policies, saved beside the model list |
| `{configDir}/addons.json` | Whether you have switched a module off — distinct from whether it is installed |
| `{cacheDir}/capability.json` | Local-model capability probe results |
| `{cacheDir}/obsidian-vault/<hash>.index.json` | The entity index derived from your Obsidian vault, written when you save the vault settings or press **Reindex vault**. Never written into the vault itself |
| `{configDir}/obsidian-vault.json` | Obsidian vault path and its switches |
| `<parent>/Tusks-Lore/tusks-lore.json` | Marker file for the shared sibling Tusk's Lore folder (auto-detected; created by the **Create Tusk's Lore** button under Tome of Lore → Lore source) |
| `<parent>/Tusks-Lore/Sessions/<campaign>/Session-NN-YYYY-MM-DD-<full\|condensed>.docx` | Structured `.docx` chronicle exports written by the in-app "Save to Tusk's Lore" buttons |
| `~/.cache/huggingface/hub` (`%USERPROFILE%\.cache\huggingface\hub` on Windows; `HF_HOME` moves it) | Whisper model weights (about 3 GB), downloaded on your first transcription (safe to delete: they download again) |
| `<repo>/vendor/python-venv/` | Whisper sidecar (faster-whisper + torch) — only present when Audio Transcription is installed |
| `<repo>/.env` | Optional `VITE_` / `PAID_` keys and model overrides for the browser build |

`{configDir}`, `{dataDir}` and `{cacheDir}` resolve to:

- Windows — `%APPDATA%\tusks-tomes\Config\` (Roaming, not Local — `env-paths` puts config under `%APPDATA%`), `%LOCALAPPDATA%\tusks-tomes\Data\` and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\tusks-tomes\Cache\`
- macOS — `~/Library/Preferences/tusks-tomes/`, `~/Library/Application Support/tusks-tomes/` and `~/Library/Caches/tusks-tomes/`
- Linux — `~/.config/tusks-tomes/`, `~/.local/share/tusks-tomes/` and `~/.cache/tusks-tomes/` (`XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, `XDG_DATA_HOME` and `XDG_CACHE_HOME` move them)

The app has no variable of its own for the config, data and cache folders; only the sessions folder can be moved (`TUSKS_SESSIONS_DIR`).

The keystore being machine-bound means a leaked `providers.enc` does not decrypt on a machine with a different host name or user name. See [privacy.md](../security/overview.md) for the full trust model.


</div>
</details>

<details class="docs-section">
<summary><h2>Useful environment variables</h2></summary>
<div class="docs-section-body">


| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `PAID_GEMINI_API_KEY` | Billing-enabled Gemini key (required for Gemini 3.x) |
| `VITE_GEMINI_API_KEY` | Free-tier Gemini fallback |
| `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | OpenRouter key seed — one key reaches around 400 models |
| `VITE_MODEL_PRO` / `VITE_MODEL_FLASH` | Override default Gemini model IDs |
| `PORT` | Dev server port (default 5173) |
| `TUSKS_HOST` | Interface to bind (default `127.0.0.1`). Set to `0.0.0.0` to expose to LAN — see the callout below before doing this |
| `TUSKS_LAN_WRITES` | When set with `TUSKS_HOST=0.0.0.0`: also allow **writes** (uploads, settings edits, saves) from other LAN devices. Default OFF — LAN visitors can only READ. Set to `1` to enable. See the callout below |
| `TUSKS_SESSIONS_DIR` | Override where multi-GB session audio lives |
| `TUSKS_VAULT_DIR` | Override sister-Vault auto-detect path (see [vault.md](../extras/tusks-vault.md)) |
| `TUSKS_LORE_DIR` | Override the sibling `Tusks-Lore/` auto-detect path. The folder holds `tusks-lore.json` (marker) + `Sessions/<campaign>/*.docx` (chronicle archive); same folder is read by Tusk's Vault for the shared lore base |

Variables prefixed with `VITE_` or `PAID_` are read from `.env` and inlined into the browser bundle by Vite (configured via `envPrefix` in `vite.config.ts`); keys saved in Settings are not part of the bundle. Every other variable is read by the server from your real environment, not from `.env`, and plain-named ones (like `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`) are not placed in the bundle.

> [!CAUTION]
> **Before you set `TUSKS_HOST=0.0.0.0`, read this.** It exposes Tusk's Tomes
> to your local network. Useful at home; **dangerous on hotel, café, airport or
> coworking Wi-Fi**, where the "same Wi-Fi" attacker is real and doesn't need
> to be technical — pointing a browser at your IP is enough.

The trade-offs in plain English:

Other devices (a tablet, your partner's laptop, your phone) can open the app at `http://<your-machine-IP>:5173`.

- Your API keys are **still safe**. The `/api/provider-keys` route is loopback-only regardless of `TUSKS_HOST`. Devices visiting from elsewhere on the LAN get a 403 on that route. Your stored Gemini, OpenRouter and runner credentials are never served to other devices.
- **LAN writes are OFF by default.** Other devices can BROWSE chronicles, transcripts, and session lists. They cannot upload audio, save chronicles, edit the glossary or routing, or modify anything else unless you also set `TUSKS_LAN_WRITES=1`. Saving the app's own settings, and everything that touches your keys, stays on the host either way. So if a stranger gets onto your Wi-Fi by accident, they can look but not touch.
- **Everything readable IS visible to anyone on the same Wi-Fi.** Transcripts in progress, finished chronicles, your campaign + session metadata — anyone who can reach your IP can browse them.

If you also want to **upload from your phone, drag transcripts in from another machine, or edit the glossary from a tablet**, set `TUSKS_LAN_WRITES=1` in addition to `TUSKS_HOST=0.0.0.0`. This opens the write surface to every LAN device — only do it on networks where you trust every connected device. The app prints a loud warning at boot when this is on.

If you only need to read chronicles from another device, consider exporting the chronicle as a `.docx` from the Sessions tab and emailing it to yourself instead. That avoids LAN exposure entirely.

For the full security picture (keystore machine-binding, what runs over the network, residual risks we cannot fix in code), see [security-quickref.md](../security/overview.md).


</div>
</details>

<details class="docs-section">
<summary><h2>What a fresh clone contains</h2></summary>
<div class="docs-section-body">


Source code, setup scripts, the launcher, and configuration **templates only**. Nothing in this list contains personal data or credentials.


</div>
</details>

<details class="docs-section">
<summary><h2>What gets created at runtime</h2></summary>
<div class="docs-section-body">


`node_modules/`, optionally the Python environment (Audio Transcription), `Sessions/`, the encrypted keystore, the settings JSONs listed above, `.env`, model caches, session manifests — all gitignored.


</div>
</details>

<details class="docs-section">
<summary><h2>Pacing & chunk sizes</h2></summary>
<div class="docs-section-body">


Pacing between cloud chunks is **automatic and per-provider**. The delay before each chunk is `max(60 s ÷ requests per minute, input tokens ÷ tokens per minute × 60 s) × 1.1`, less the time since the last call, and the **Slow down** option in the rate-limit dialog multiplies it by 3. Gemini uses a static table keyed on the key tier (paid or free) and the model (Pro or Flash): paid Pro 150 requests and 2,000,000 tokens a minute, paid Flash 1,000 and 4,000,000, free Pro 2 and 32,000, free Flash 10 and 250,000. OpenRouter is paced on requests per minute only: 20 for `:free` models and a nominal 60 for the rest. A 429 `Retry-After` is honoured.

Per-provider chunk sizes live in `src/features/pipeline/lib/chunking.ts`:

Sizes are keyed on **(provider profile, model tier)**, not on the provider
alone. A fast-tier model runs chunks roughly half the flagship size: cheaper per
call, and it degrades less on long inputs, so quality holds at lower token
counts. Figures below are the flagship row, in chars, for Phase 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 / 5:

- Gemini paid: 30k / 30k / 60k / 60k / 100k
- Gemini free: 15k / 15k / 35k / 35k / 60k (throughput-tight)
- Claude profile (Claude Code): 20k / 20k / 40k / 40k / 60k
- OpenAI profile (Codex): 15k / 15k / 30k / 30k / 50k — OpenRouter maps onto this row
- Local (any runner): 5k / 5k / 8k / 8k / 10k, plus 6k for Phase 3.5, which only local runs use — conservative; consumer GPUs lose accuracy on long contexts

Override by editing the constants — no env var. The rate-limit state itself is in `src/features/providers/lib/rateLimit.ts` and is per-provider singleton.


</div>
</details>

<details class="docs-section">
<summary><h2>Model list updates</h2></summary>
<div class="docs-section-body">

**Keep the model list up to date automatically** (Settings, Providers and models, under Model lists) is on by default. The app keeps a copy of OpenRouter's public model list, with prices and context sizes, and asks `openrouter.ai` for a newer one at most once a day. Cost estimates, chunk sizes, output limits and the model picker all read that copy, so new models and price changes show up without you doing anything. The request is anonymous and carries no key, transcript or lore. OpenRouter's list of each provider's data policy (whether it trains on or keeps your prompts) is kept the same way, beside the model list.

Turn it off and the app never contacts `openrouter.ai` for the list by itself. It keeps using the copy it has, however old, until you press **Re-check** on the Model lists strip. If a check fails (offline, or OpenRouter is down), the saved list keeps working, is marked as stale, and the app waits an hour before trying again, doubling the wait up to a day. With no saved list and no connection the app still runs; model prices and limits then fall back to built-in defaults.

</div>
</details>

<details class="docs-section">
<summary><h2>Updating</h2></summary>
<div class="docs-section-body">


The in-app updater lives at **Settings → Maintenance → Check for updates → Apply update**. One click pulls the latest code from `main` (fast-forward only, and only on a clean checkout of `main`) and prompts you to restart. When the dependencies changed, it shows the `npm install` command to run after you stop the app. Your encrypted keystore, sessions, glossary, lore, and other gitignored state survive untouched.

Prefer the terminal?

```sh
git pull && npm install
```

Either path requires Git installed locally. If you downloaded the ZIP and don't have Git, the cleanest update path is to re-download the ZIP from GitHub and unzip over your existing folder — your gitignored files survive that too.

Updates are **free, optional, and never required**. If a release breaks something for you, just don't update yet — the version you have keeps working.


</div>
</details>
